You need to write a spec for a **three-layer measurement front-end**.

Not a theory spec. An engineering spec.

## The three things to design

### 1. Linear branch-intensity generator

This is the passive front-end that takes the prepared state and produces physical branch intensities.

Its job is:

* accept the stored resonant state from the shared core
* apply the analyzer settings
* expose physical output branches
* guarantee branch absorbed-power envelopes proportional to the target weights

Single-particle version:
[
p_i(t)\propto w_i
]

Joint version:
[
p_{xy}(t)\propto w_{xy}(a,b)
]

This block is basically:

* shared core
* analyzer couplers
* passive output branches

### 2. Stochastic nucleation element

This is the real missing detector physics.

Its job is:

* sit on each output branch
* remain quiescent under sub-threshold branch activity
* undergo a rare irreversible initiation event
* have initiation hazard approximately proportional to branch absorbed intensity

Target behavior:
[
\lambda_i(t)\approx \kappa,p_i(t)
]
or after normalization
[
\lambda_i(t)=\gamma(t),w_i
]

This is the hardest block.

### 3. Common-mode / zero-sequence latch

This is the post-click completion block.

Its job is:

* detect that one branch has nucleated
* suppress all other branches quickly
* open a strong drain path for the winner
* route remaining stored energy into the winning branch
* produce a single macroscopic recorded outcome

This is not where Born comes from. This is where **one-click exclusivity** comes from.

---

# So what spec should you write?

I would write **one engineering spec with three subcircuits**.

## Subcircuit A — Analyzer/readout network

### Inputs

* prepared resonant state from shared core
* analyzer settings (a,b)

### Outputs

* branch voltages/currents for
  [
  ++,\ +-,\ -+,\ --
  ]

### Requirement

Before any detector nonlinearity,
[
p_k(t)=v_k(t)i_k(t)
]
must satisfy
[
p_k(t)=\Gamma(t),w_k(a,b)
]
to within tolerance, with a common envelope (\Gamma(t)).

### Acceptance metric

Normalized absorbed energies with linear resistive loads:
[
f_k=\frac{E_k}{\sum_j E_j}
]
must match (w_k).

So this block proves the front-end computes the right weights.

---

## Subcircuit B — Nucleation detector cell

One copy per branch.

### Inputs

* local branch voltage/current or absorbed power signal

### Output

* binary nucleation event

### Required behavior

* no continuous analog output is the recorded outcome
* branch should produce a **rare discrete initiation**
* hazard should be approximately linear in absorbed branch power over operating range

Engineering target:
[
\lambda_k \approx \alpha,p_k
]

### Candidate implementations

* avalanche trigger
* metastable latch biased near instability
* breakdown element
* tunneling/noise-assisted trigger
* shot-noise absorber with one-shot commit

### What to characterize

* hazard vs absorbed power curve
* dead time / reset
* timing jitter
* dark-count rate
* branch-to-branch matching

### Acceptance metric

Across calibrated operating range,
[
\lambda_k / p_k
]
should be approximately constant and matched across branches.

This is the most important spec.

---

## Subcircuit C — Zero-sequence/common-mode latch

Shared across all branches.

### Inputs

* branch nucleation flags

### Outputs

* winner latch
* loser suppression
* winner drain enable

### Required behavior

Once branch (k) nucleates:

* all other branches are inhibited fast
* winner drain path turns on
* remaining shared stored energy is extracted through winner
* only one outcome is recorded

### Physical interpretation

This is the common-mode/zero-sequence closure channel.

### Acceptance metric

* one nucleation event leads to one and only one final recorded winner
* losing branches absorb negligible post-click energy
* winner absorbs nearly all remaining reservoir energy

# The actual engineering document outline

## Section 1 — Functional decomposition

Describe the three blocks:

1. branch-weight generator
2. nucleation detector
3. common latch/closure

## Section 2 — Signals and interfaces

Define:

* resonant input ports
* analyzer controls
* branch output ports
* nucleation event signal
* latch signal
* winner drain signal

## Section 3 — Quantitative requirements

### Front-end

[
p_k(t)=\Gamma(t)w_k + \text{error}
]
with branch-weight error tolerance.

### Detector cell

[
\lambda_k \approx \alpha p_k
]
with linearity tolerance and matching tolerance.

### Latch

Winner-take-all settling time, suppression ratio, and post-click energy-capture requirement.

## Section 4 — Test plan

Three separate tests:

### Test A: linear front-end only

Replace detectors with resistors and verify (f_k\approx w_k).

### Test B: single detector-cell characterization

Drive one branch with controlled absorbed power and fit (\lambda(p)).

### Test C: full competition

Run all branches together, verify:

* one winner per trial
* loser suppression
* winner frequency tracks target weights

# What specifically has to be designed

Here is the blunt list.

## Must design now

* analyzer/readout coupler network
* branch detector cell
* common latch/closure network
* measurement/reset procedure

## Must choose now

* what physical effect provides nucleation
* what physical variable the latch watches
* what component implements loser suppression
* what component opens winner drain

## Can postpone

* exact tank hardware realization of the shared core
* full SPICE of the entire apparatus
* entanglement-scale 4-branch build

Because until the detector cell is specified, the rest is premature.

# The most important design question

The single most important engineering question is:

> **What physical device gives you a nucleation rate approximately proportional to absorbed branch power?**

That is the heart of the detector layer.

Everything else is easier.
